summary:
On long missions, astronauts must monitor and manage their own health, far from medical support and with delayed communication to Earth. Sirius is a single health hub for every piece of on-board hardware that can track health: wearables, exercise equipment, radiation dosimeters and medical devices.

Each device connects through its own adapter, which converts its data into one standard format (IEEE 1752.1 / Open mHealth). Adding new hardware takes one new adapter and nothing else. Our live demo streams simulated wearables and radiation badges for a crew of six. A dashboard turns the data into three scores, Recovery, Radiation and Mind. Alerts follow a five-tier escalation model based on the clinical NEWS2 early-warning system and on each astronaut’s own normal. Each alert gives a clear next step. Sirius also includes a 3D body map, a health log aligned with NASA monitoring schedules, daily cognitive tests, a crew-wide view and a flight surgeon mode.

Combining every device reveals problems no single sensor can detect. This gives crews the information to recognise problems early and act on their own health, which future Moon and Mars missions will require.
details:
Sirius: health on board, by The Tylonauts

What it does

On long missions, astronauts must monitor their own health while far from medical support and facing communication delays with Earth. Sirius is a health hub that combines data from an astronaut’s wearables and on-board exercise equipment into one centralised platform.

Wearables (a smart watch, a smart shirt and a radiation badge) send readings to a cloud backend. There, a separate adapter for each device type converts them into one standard format (IEEE 1752.1 / Open mHealth). On-board exercise equipment, such as the ISS’s resistance trainer (ARED), cycle ergometer (CEVIS) and treadmill (T2), is designed to connect the same way. It would add exercise sessions, load and exercise heart rate, which matter for countering muscle, bone and cardiovascular loss in microgravity.

The dashboard turns these readings into three scores, Recovery, Radiation and Mind, each rated Steady, Watch or Alert. A five-tier escalation system, based on the clinical NEWS2 early-warning chart and on each astronaut’s own normal, raises alerts that state the issue and what to do next.

Sirius also includes:

- a 3D body map highlighting areas that need attention

- a health log scheduled to NASA’s published monitoring schedules

- short daily cognitive tests

- a hands-off voice summary

- a crew view that detects problems several crew members share

- a detailed view for flight surgeons

Benefits and intended impact

Each device sees only part of the body. Combining wearables with exercise equipment lets readings be cross-checked and reveals patterns no single device can show, for example a reduced exercise load combined with poor recovery. Sirius turns raw data into a few scores and plain advice, judged against each person’s own normal. This lets crews spot problems such as poor sleep, low oxygen, radiation build-up or falling mood early, and act on them without waiting for Earth. Any new wearable or exercise device is added through a single adapter, so the system can grow with future hardware. The same approach could serve other remote, isolated settings, such as polar stations and submarines.

Tools and technologies

Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, three.js (with the BodyParts3D anatomy model, CC BY 4.0) and the Web Speech API.

Backend: Python with FastAPI, Neon Postgres, hosted on Vercel.

Simulation: 18 simulated wearables for a crew of six, controlled live (stress, hypoxia, radiation, solar storms, sensor faults), and a Python script that generates 30 days of history.

Collaboration: GitHub.

Hardware: none. All devices are simulated because real astronaut health data is not public.

Creativity

Sirius is built around the many devices that astronauts already use, bringing personal wearables and shared exercise equipment into one view. It detects health trends across the whole crew, which point to shared causes rather than one person’s illness. It turns NASA-style cognitive testing into a daily habit. Its live simulation lets judges trigger events such as a solar storm and watch the system respond.

Factors considered

We based our health metrics on NASA’s Human Research Program hazards, NASA-STD-3001 requirements (such as the 600 mSv career radiation limit), NASA’s exercise countermeasures (about 600 minutes per week) and published monitoring schedules.

We also designed for:

- communication delays, so the app works without help from the ground

- crew privacy: sensitive health info shared only with the doctor, not other crew members

- accessibility, with status always shown as an icon and a word, never colour alone

- transparency, with simulated data and placeholder formulas clearly labelled

Use of AI tools

Claude (Anthropic) assisted with code, documentation, research summaries and the code that generates the simulated data. AI-assisted commits are marked in the project’s Git history. The voice feature uses the browser’s built-in text-to-speech with answers scripted by the team. The project contains no NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.
